lessons.title: Stars and Galaxies
lessons.content: What is a star, and how does it produce light and heat? A star is a massive ball of hot gas (mostly hydrogen and helium) that produces enormous amounts of energy through nuclear fusion in its core, where hydrogen atoms combine to form helium, releasing huge amounts of light and heat — our Sun is a star, just much closer to us than any other. What is a galaxy? A galaxy is an enormous collection of billions of stars, along with gas, dust, and dark matter, all held together by gravity — our Sun and solar system are part of the Milky Way galaxy. What is the life cycle of a star, in broad terms? A star forms from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust (a nebula); it spends most of its life fusing hydrogen into helium in a stable stage; once its fuel runs low, smaller stars expand into a red giant then shrink into a white dwarf, while much larger stars explode as a supernova, potentially leaving behind a neutron star or a black hole. Why do stars appear as tiny points of light, despite being enormous? Stars are so incredibly far away that even though they are vastly larger than the Earth, their apparent size in the sky is reduced to a point — this vast distance is why light from distant stars takes years (measured in light-years, the distance light travels in one year) to reach us. What is the difference between a star and a planet as seen in the night sky? Stars produce their own light through nuclear fusion and tend to twinkle due to atmospheric disturbance, while planets shine only by reflecting sunlight and generally appear as steadier, non-twinkling points of light.
examples:
Explain why the Sun appears far larger and brighter in our sky than any other star.
Step 1: Recall all other stars are vastly further away than the Sun
Step 2: Consider how distance affects apparent size and brightness
Answer: The Sun only appears larger and brighter because it is enormously closer to Earth than any other star, not because it is bigger

Describe what a light-year measures.
Step 1: Recall a light-year is a unit of distance, not time
Step 2: Recall it is defined by how far light travels in one year
Answer: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, used to measure the vast distances between stars

Explain what powers a star's light and heat output.
Step 1: Recall nuclear fusion occurs in a star's core
Step 2: Recall hydrogen atoms combine to form helium, releasing energy
Answer: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium in the star's core releases enormous amounts of energy as light and heat

Describe the difference in appearance between a star and a planet in the night sky.
Step 1: Recall stars produce their own light and tend to twinkle
Step 2: Recall planets only reflect sunlight and appear steadier
Answer: Stars twinkle due to atmospheric disturbance of their own emitted light, while planets shine with steadier reflected light and generally do not twinkle

Describe what happens to a very large star once it runs out of nuclear fuel.
Step 1: Recall large stars expand and then explode dramatically
Step 2: Recall what can remain after the explosion
Answer: A very large star explodes as a supernova, potentially leaving behind an extremely dense neutron star or, for the largest stars, a black hole

lessons.title: Satellites and Communication
lessons.content: What is a satellite, and what are the two main categories? A satellite is any object that orbits a larger body due to gravity — natural satellites (like the Moon orbiting Earth) occur without human involvement, while artificial satellites are human-made objects launched into orbit for specific purposes, such as communication, weather monitoring, navigation (GPS), or scientific research. What is a geostationary orbit, and why is it useful? A geostationary orbit is a specific circular orbit (directly above the equator, at a set altitude) where a satellite orbits at exactly the same rate as the Earth rotates, so it appears to stay fixed above the same point on Earth's surface at all times — this makes geostationary satellites ideal for continuous communication and television broadcasting, since a ground dish can stay pointed at one fixed spot in the sky. How do communication satellites work? A signal is transmitted up from a ground station (uplink) to the satellite, which receives it, boosts its strength, and retransmits it back down to a different location on Earth (downlink) — this lets signals travel across vast distances and around the curve of the Earth, well beyond the reach of direct line-of-sight ground transmission. What is a low Earth orbit satellite, and what is it used for? Low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites orbit much closer to Earth and complete an orbit in a much shorter time (often under two hours), moving across the sky relative to the ground — these are commonly used for Earth observation, weather imaging, and increasingly for satellite internet, requiring many satellites working together since each one is only overhead briefly. How has satellite technology impacted Uganda and similar countries? Satellite communication and GPS navigation allow remote or rural areas without extensive ground infrastructure (like cables) to access phone networks, television, internet, and accurate positioning, helping to bridge the digital divide.
examples:
Explain why a geostationary satellite is well suited to broadcasting television signals continuously to one region.
Step 1: Recall a geostationary satellite stays above the same point on Earth at all times
Step 2: Consider what this means for a fixed ground-based satellite dish
Answer: Because the satellite always stays in the same position relative to the ground, a dish can remain permanently pointed at it without needing to track its movement

Describe the path a communication signal follows from a football match broadcast to a viewer's home.
Step 1: Recall the uplink from the ground station to the satellite
Step 2: Recall the downlink from the satellite to the receiving location
Answer: The signal is transmitted up (uplink) to the satellite, boosted, and sent back down (downlink) to be received by television providers and eventually broadcast to homes

Explain why several low Earth orbit satellites are needed together to provide continuous internet coverage, unlike a single geostationary satellite.
Step 1: Recall LEO satellites orbit quickly and move across the sky relative to the ground
Step 2: Consider that each LEO satellite is only overhead for a short time
Answer: Since each LEO satellite passes overhead only briefly before moving on, many must work together in a coordinated network to ensure at least one is always in range

Explain how satellite technology can help a remote village without any telephone cables gain access to a phone network.
Step 1: Recall satellites can transmit signals without needing ground-based cables
Step 2: Consider a receiving station or device that connects directly to the satellite
Answer: A satellite can send and receive signals directly to a village's receiving equipment, giving it phone or internet access without needing miles of cable infrastructure

Distinguish between a natural and an artificial satellite, giving one example of each.
Step 1: Recall natural satellites occur without human involvement
Step 2: Recall artificial satellites are human-made and launched into orbit
Answer: The Moon is a natural satellite of Earth, while a communication or weather satellite launched by a space agency is an artificial satellite

lessons.title: Introduction to Current Electricity
lessons.content: What is electric current, and what causes it to flow? Electric current is the flow of electric charge (carried by electrons in a conductor) around a complete circuit, measured in amperes (A) — current only flows when there is a complete, unbroken path (circuit) and a source of energy, like a battery, to push the charges around. What is the difference between a series and a parallel circuit? In a series circuit, components are connected one after another in a single loop, so the same current flows through every component, and if one component fails or is removed, the whole circuit is broken; in a parallel circuit, components are connected across separate branches, so current can take multiple paths, meaning each branch can be switched independently and the current splits between them according to each branch's resistance. What basic circuit components and symbols should be recognised? A cell/battery (the energy source), a switch (opens or closes the circuit), a resistor (limits current flow), an ammeter (measures current, connected in series), a voltmeter (measures potential difference, connected in parallel across a component), and a bulb/lamp (converts electrical energy to light). What is the difference between conductors and insulators? Conductors (like copper and other metals) allow electric charge to flow through them easily, because they have free electrons; insulators (like rubber, plastic, and glass) do not allow charge to flow easily, which is why electrical wires are covered in insulating plastic for safety.
examples:
State what happens to the other bulbs in a series circuit if one bulb burns out.
Step 1: Recall a series circuit has only one path for current
Step 2: Consider what a broken bulb does to that single path
Answer: All the bulbs go out, since the broken bulb breaks the only current path in the circuit

State what happens to the other bulbs in a parallel circuit if one bulb burns out.
Step 1: Recall a parallel circuit has separate branches for current
Step 2: Consider that other branches remain complete
Answer: The other bulbs stay lit, since each branch operates independently in a parallel circuit

Identify the correct way to connect an ammeter in a circuit to measure current.
Step 1: Recall an ammeter measures the current flowing through a component
Step 2: Recall this requires being part of the same current path
Answer: An ammeter must be connected in series with the component being measured

Identify the correct way to connect a voltmeter to measure the potential difference across a bulb.
Step 1: Recall a voltmeter measures potential difference between two points
Step 2: Recall this requires connecting across (parallel to) the component
Answer: A voltmeter must be connected in parallel across the bulb

Explain why electrical wires are covered in plastic rather than left as bare metal.
Step 1: Recall metal is a good conductor, plastic is a good insulator
Step 2: Consider the risk of a person touching bare, current-carrying metal
Answer: The plastic insulation prevents electric current from flowing into anyone who touches the wire, protecting against electric shock

lessons.title: Voltage, Resistance and Ohm's Law
lessons.content: What is voltage (potential difference), and what does it represent? Voltage, also called potential difference, is the amount of electrical energy transferred per unit of charge as it moves between two points in a circuit, measured in volts (V) — it represents the 'push' driving current around the circuit, similar to how pressure drives water through a pipe. What is resistance, and what factors affect it? Resistance is a measure of how much a component opposes the flow of electric current, measured in ohms (Ω) — a longer or thinner conductor, or one made from a material with naturally higher resistance, will have greater resistance, restricting current flow more. What does Ohm's Law state, and how is it used? For many conductors at constant temperature, voltage is directly proportional to current, expressed as Voltage = Current × Resistance (V = IR) — this means for a fixed resistance, doubling the voltage doubles the current, and the formula can be rearranged to find any one of the three quantities if the other two are known. How does total resistance behave in series versus parallel circuits? In series, resistances simply add together to give the total resistance (R_total = R1 + R2 + ...), since the current must pass through each one in turn; in parallel, adding more resistors actually DECREASES the total resistance, since each additional branch gives current more alternative paths to flow through.
examples:
Find the current through a 20Ω resistor connected to a 10V supply.
Step 1: Use V = IR, rearranged to I = V/R
Step 2: Substitute: 10÷20
Answer: Current = 0.5A

Find the voltage across a 15Ω resistor carrying a current of 2A.
Step 1: Use V = IR
Step 2: Substitute: 2×15
Answer: Voltage = 30V

Find the resistance of a component that has 12V across it and carries a current of 3A.
Step 1: Use V = IR, rearranged to R = V/I
Step 2: Substitute: 12÷3
Answer: Resistance = 4Ω

Two resistors of 5Ω and 8Ω are connected in series. Find the total resistance.
Step 1: Recall series resistances simply add
Step 2: Add: 5+8
Answer: Total resistance = 13Ω

Explain why adding another resistor in parallel to an existing one decreases the circuit's total resistance, rather than increasing it.
Step 1: Recall each parallel branch offers current an additional path
Step 2: Consider that more available paths make it easier overall for current to flow
Answer: Because current has more alternative paths to take, the overall opposition to current flow decreases, so total resistance goes down even though more components have been added

lessons.title: Electromagnetic Effects
lessons.content: What is electromagnetic induction? The generation of an electric current in a conductor caused by a changing magnetic field around it — this happens whenever a conductor moves through a magnetic field, or a magnetic field near a conductor changes strength, and it is the basic principle behind how generators produce electricity. What factors increase the size of an induced current? A stronger magnet, a faster relative movement between the conductor and the magnetic field, and more turns of wire in a coil all increase the induced current — this relationship is used in the design of practical generators and dynamos. How does an electric motor work? An electric motor uses the opposite effect of induction: when a current-carrying wire is placed in a magnetic field, it experiences a force (this is sometimes called the motor effect) — in a simple motor, a coil carrying current sits within a magnetic field, and the resulting force on each side of the coil creates a continuous turning effect, converting electrical energy into mechanical (rotational) motion. What is the difference between a simple generator and a motor in terms of energy conversion? A generator converts mechanical energy (motion) INTO electrical energy through electromagnetic induction; a motor converts electrical energy INTO mechanical energy through the motor effect — they use the same core electromagnetic principles, but in opposite directions. How does a transformer use electromagnetic induction? A transformer uses a changing current in one coil (the primary) to induce a changing magnetic field, which then induces a current in a nearby second coil (the secondary) — this only works with alternating current (AC), since direct current (DC) produces no changing magnetic field to induce anything.
examples:
State what happens to the induced current if a magnet is pushed into a coil faster.
Step 1: Recall faster relative movement increases induced current
Answer: The induced current increases

State what happens to the induced current if a coil has more turns of wire, for the same magnet movement.
Step 1: Recall more turns increase the induced current
Answer: The induced current increases

Explain the basic energy conversion that occurs inside an electric generator.
Step 1: Recall a generator uses electromagnetic induction
Step 2: Identify what type of energy goes in, and what comes out
Answer: A generator converts mechanical energy (motion, e.g. turning a coil) into electrical energy

Explain the basic energy conversion that occurs inside an electric motor.
Step 1: Recall a motor uses the motor effect (force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field)
Step 2: Identify what type of energy goes in, and what comes out
Answer: A motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy (motion)

Explain why a transformer does not work with direct current (DC).
Step 1: Recall a transformer relies on a changing magnetic field to induce current in the secondary coil
Step 2: Recall DC produces a constant (unchanging) magnetic field
Answer: Since DC does not produce a changing magnetic field, no current can be induced in the secondary coil, so transformers only work with alternating current (AC)

lessons.title: Electric Energy Distribution and Consumption
lessons.content: How is electrical energy generated and transported from a power station to homes? Power stations generate electricity, which then passes through step-up transformers to a very high voltage for transmission across the national grid — transmitting at high voltage (and correspondingly low current) greatly reduces energy lost as heat in the cables, since power loss depends on the SQUARE of the current; step-down transformers then reduce the voltage to safe levels before it reaches homes and businesses. How is the electrical energy used by an appliance calculated? Electrical power is calculated as Power = Voltage × Current (P = VI), measured in watts; the total energy consumed over time is Energy = Power × Time (E = Pt), often measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh) for billing purposes, where 1 kWh is the energy used by a 1000W appliance running for 1 hour. Why is it more efficient to transmit electricity at high voltage over long distances? Since power loss in a cable equals (current)² × resistance, transmitting the same power at a much higher voltage requires a much lower current, drastically cutting the energy wasted as heat in the transmission cables. What are some ways to use electrical energy more efficiently at home? Switching off appliances and lights when not in use, using energy-efficient bulbs (like LEDs, which convert more electrical energy into light and less into wasted heat), and choosing appliances with a good energy efficiency rating all reduce electricity consumption and cost.
examples:
Find the power consumed by an appliance operating at 240V with a current of 5A.
Step 1: Use P = VI
Step 2: Substitute: 240×5
Answer: Power = 1200W

Find the energy consumed by a 2000W heater running for 3 hours.
Step 1: Use E = Pt
Step 2: Substitute: 2000×3
Answer: Energy = 6000Wh = 6kWh

A household uses 15kWh of electricity in a day at a cost of UGX 700 per kWh. Find the total cost.
Step 1: Multiply energy used by cost per unit: 15×700
Answer: Total cost = UGX 10,500

Explain why power is transmitted across the national grid at very high voltage rather than low voltage.
Step 1: Recall power loss in a cable depends on current squared
Step 2: Recall a higher voltage means a lower current for the same transmitted power
Answer: Transmitting at high voltage keeps the current low, and since power loss depends on current squared, this greatly reduces the energy wasted as heat in the cables

Explain why switching from ordinary bulbs to LED bulbs reduces a household's electricity bill.
Step 1: Recall LEDs convert more electrical energy into light and less into wasted heat
Step 2: Consider that less energy used means lower energy cost over time
Answer: LEDs are more efficient at converting electrical energy into light, so they use less power for the same brightness, reducing the total energy consumed and therefore the electricity bill

lessons.title: Atomic Models
lessons.content: How has the scientific model of the atom changed over time? Early models pictured the atom as a solid, indivisible sphere; J.J. Thomson's 'plum pudding' model proposed a positively charged sphere with negatively charged electrons scattered through it; Ernest Rutherford's gold foil experiment (firing alpha particles at thin gold foil, and observing that most passed straight through but a small number bounced back sharply) revealed that an atom is mostly empty space with a small, dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre; Niels Bohr then refined this by proposing that electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed, defined energy levels (shells), rather than moving randomly. What are the three main subatomic particles, and their properties? Protons (positive charge, found in the nucleus), neutrons (no charge, also found in the nucleus), and electrons (negative charge, found in shells orbiting the nucleus) — protons and neutrons have approximately equal, much larger mass than electrons, which is why almost all of an atom's mass is concentrated in its tiny nucleus. What do atomic number and mass number tell you about an atom? The atomic number equals the number of protons (and, in a neutral atom, also the number of electrons), and uniquely identifies which element the atom is; the mass number equals the total number of protons plus neutrons in the nucleus. What is an isotope? Atoms of the same element (same atomic number, same number of protons) that have a different number of neutrons, and therefore a different mass number — isotopes of the same element behave almost identically chemically, but can have very different physical and nuclear properties.
examples:
Describe what Rutherford's gold foil experiment revealed about the structure of the atom.
Step 1: Recall most alpha particles passed straight through the foil
Step 2: Recall a small number bounced back sharply
Answer: The atom is mostly empty space, with a small, dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre that occasionally deflects alpha particles

An atom has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. Find its mass number.
Step 1: Use mass number = protons + neutrons
Step 2: Substitute: 11+12
Answer: Mass number = 23

An atom has atomic number 8 and mass number 16. Find the number of neutrons.
Step 1: Recall neutrons = mass number − atomic number (protons)
Step 2: Substitute: 16−8
Answer: Number of neutrons = 8

Two atoms of the same element have mass numbers 12 and 14. Explain what this tells you about them.
Step 1: Recall isotopes share the same atomic number (protons) but differ in neutrons
Step 2: Consider that different mass numbers with the same element mean different neutron counts
Answer: These are isotopes of the same element — they have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons

State the charge and location of a neutron within an atom.
Step 1: Recall a neutron has no electric charge
Step 2: Recall neutrons are found in the nucleus, alongside protons
Answer: A neutron has no charge and is located in the nucleus

lessons.title: Nuclear Processes
lessons.content: What is radioactivity, and why do some atomic nuclei undergo it? Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of particles or energy from an unstable atomic nucleus as it changes into a more stable configuration — this happens in isotopes whose combination of protons and neutrons makes the nucleus unstable. What are the three main types of radioactive emission, and how do they differ? Alpha particles (two protons and two neutrons, relatively large and heavy, stopped by just a sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air); beta particles (fast-moving electrons, more penetrating than alpha, stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium); and gamma rays (high-energy electromagnetic waves, the most penetrating, requiring thick lead or concrete to significantly reduce them). What is half-life? The time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay — half-life is constant for a given isotope regardless of the sample's size, and after each half-life period, the remaining radioactivity is halved again. What is nuclear fission, and where is it used? Fission is the splitting of a large, unstable nucleus (like uranium-235) into two smaller nuclei, releasing a large amount of energy — this is the process used in nuclear power stations to generate electricity, and in a controlled chain reaction, one fission event can trigger further fission events. What safety precautions are needed when handling radioactive materials? Minimising exposure time, keeping as much distance as possible from the source, and using appropriate shielding (like lead) all reduce the radiation dose received, since radiation exposure decreases sharply with distance and shielding.
examples:
State which type of radioactive emission is stopped by just a sheet of paper.
Step 1: Recall alpha particles are large, heavy, and easily stopped
Answer: Alpha particles

State which type of radioactive emission requires thick lead or concrete to significantly reduce it.
Step 1: Recall gamma rays are the most penetrating form of radiation
Answer: Gamma rays

A radioactive sample has a half-life of 5 years and starts with 80g of radioactive material. Find how much remains after 15 years.
Step 1: Find how many half-lives have passed: 15÷5=3 half-lives
Step 2: Halve the amount three times: 80→40→20→10
Answer: 10g remains after 15 years

A sample starts with 100g of a radioactive isotope with a half-life of 10 years. Find how much remains after 20 years.
Step 1: Find the number of half-lives: 20÷10=2
Step 2: Halve the amount twice: 100→50→25
Answer: 25g remains after 20 years

Explain two ways a laboratory worker can reduce their radiation exposure when handling a radioactive source.
Step 1: Recall exposure decreases with distance from the source
Step 2: Recall shielding materials absorb radiation before it reaches the worker
Answer: The worker can increase their distance from the source and use appropriate shielding (such as lead), both of which significantly reduce the radiation dose received

lessons.title: Digital Electronics
lessons.content: What is the difference between analogue and digital signals? An analogue signal varies continuously and can take any value within a range (like a dimmer light switch); a digital signal only takes discrete, specific values — most commonly just two: HIGH (often represented as 1) and LOW (often represented as 0) — digital systems are widely used because they are more resistant to interference and easier to process and store accurately. What is a logic gate, and what are the basic types? A logic gate is an electronic component that takes one or more digital inputs and produces a single digital output based on a fixed rule — an AND gate outputs HIGH only if ALL its inputs are HIGH; an OR gate outputs HIGH if AT LEAST ONE input is HIGH; and a NOT gate (inverter) simply reverses its single input, turning HIGH into LOW and LOW into HIGH. How is a logic gate's behaviour summarised? Using a truth table, which lists every possible combination of inputs alongside the resulting output — this makes it easy to see and verify exactly how a gate behaves in every situation. What are logic gates used for in real devices? Combinations of logic gates form the basis of all digital circuits, from simple alarm systems (e.g., an AND gate that only triggers an alarm if BOTH a door sensor AND a motion sensor detect activity) to the vastly more complex processors inside computers and phones. Why are digital circuits generally preferred over analogue ones for processing and storing information? Digital signals are less affected by noise and interference (since a signal only needs to be roughly HIGH or LOW to be read correctly), and can be copied, processed, and stored without gradually losing quality, unlike analogue signals.
examples:
State the output of an AND gate with inputs 1 and 0.
Step 1: Recall an AND gate only outputs 1 if ALL inputs are 1
Step 2: Note that one input here is 0
Answer: Output = 0

State the output of an OR gate with inputs 0 and 1.
Step 1: Recall an OR gate outputs 1 if AT LEAST ONE input is 1
Step 2: Note that one input here is 1
Answer: Output = 1

State the output of a NOT gate with an input of 1.
Step 1: Recall a NOT gate reverses its input
Answer: Output = 0

A security system uses an AND gate connected to a door sensor and a motion sensor, both giving 1 when triggered. Both sensors detect activity at once. Determine if the alarm (output) activates.
Step 1: Identify both inputs as 1
Step 2: Recall an AND gate outputs 1 only when all inputs are 1
Answer: The alarm activates, since both sensor inputs are 1, satisfying the AND condition

Explain why digital signals are generally more reliable for long-distance data transmission than analogue signals.
Step 1: Recall digital signals only need to be recognised as roughly HIGH or LOW
Step 2: Recall analogue signals can be gradually distorted by interference, changing their exact value
Answer: Because digital signals only require a rough HIGH/LOW distinction, small amounts of interference don't change the interpreted value, whereas analogue signals can be permanently distorted by the same interference

keyTerms.digital signal: A signal that only takes discrete values, typically HIGH (1) or LOW (0)
keyTerms.logic gate: An electronic component producing a digital output based on a fixed rule applied to its inputs
keyTerms.truth table: A table listing every input combination of a logic gate alongside its resulting output
keyTerms.AND/OR/NOT gate: Basic logic gates: AND needs all inputs HIGH, OR needs at least one HIGH, NOT reverses its input

quiz.question: An AND gate with inputs 1 and 1 produces an output of:
quiz.explanation: AND gates output 1 only when all inputs are 1.

quiz.question: An OR gate with inputs 0 and 0 produces an output of:
quiz.explanation: OR requires at least one input to be 1; with both 0, the output is 0.

quiz.question: A NOT gate with input 0 produces an output of:
quiz.explanation: A NOT gate reverses its input: 0 becomes 1.

quiz.question: A truth table is used to:
options: Show every input combination and the resulting output of a logic gate
quiz.explanation: Truth tables summarise a gate's complete behaviour for all possible inputs.

quiz.question: Digital signals are generally preferred over analogue signals because they:
options: Are more resistant to interference and easier to store accurately
quiz.explanation: Digital HIGH/LOW values remain distinguishable even with some interference, unlike continuously varying analogue signals.
